Note: Preferred template (survives editor review verbatim ~15x): 'Here the author/speaker is speaking as if X were Y. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use...' Keep this structure; do not over-explain.
Preferred template: 'The point of this comparison is that just as X, so is Y. If it would be helpful in your language, you could ...' Editors keep ~90% of simile notes in this form.
Preferred template: 'Here, **X** represents Y. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [...]' Editors keep ~87%.

Write only for genuinely abstract/theological ideas. Editors delete ~38% overall - especially notes on common nouns (tears, pain, life, violence, salvation, anger) and on repeated occurrences. Flag a given abstract noun once per passage, not every verse; later occurrences are covered by pipeline-generated see-how / also-occurs sentences.
Content-team mandate: every passive instance still gets a note - do not drop. Historical context only: editors deleted ~55% of these in LAM/HAB poetry before the mandate.
Only write when an antecedent is genuinely ambiguous across a clause boundary. Editors delete ~43%.
Skip for ordinary possessives; write only for non-ownership relations (e.g. 'daughter of Zion'). Editors delete ~61%.
Rarely worth a note in poetry; editors delete ~78%.
Only when the rhetorical force is not obvious to a modern reader. Editors delete ~42%.
Write sparingly; editors delete ~44%.
Apply a high bar - editors delete ~50%; only supply implicit info a translator could not infer.
Genre-dependent: editors deleted 57% in HAB but kept all in LAM. Write only when the parallel line adds meaning, not for every poetic couplet.
Trim marginal cases; editors delete ~30%.

AT quality rules (supplement to the every-instance mandate): (a) When the implied agent of a divine passive is clearly God, prefer an explicit-agent alternate translation — e.g. 'God prolonged their lives' rather than 'they were given an extension of life.' (b) When a single AT does not cover the full range of a passive form, add a second option separated by 'or' — e.g. '[grew weak] or [came loose]'. Editors across DAN and AMO consistently applied both patterns when rewording existing notes.
Context: AT format for divine-passive notes — explicit agent and second AT option

Note: Additional valid trigger (beyond antecedent ambiguity): in Aramaic books (DAN, EZR), an independent subject pronoun stated separately from a verb that already carries the subject signals emphatic focus — the speaker stresses their own identity or role in contrast to others. These Aramaic emphatic-pronoun constructions warrant a writing-pronouns note explaining the emphasis function and offering an explicit-emphasis AT (e.g. 'I myself fear my lord the king'). Four editors across ZEC, DAN, and AMO added notes for this pattern.
Context: Aramaic emphatic independent pronoun — separate from antecedent-ambiguity rule

Note: ANE court regalia (purple garments, gold chains/necklaces around the neck) are symbols of high rank and authority in ancient Near Eastern culture; always add a translate-symaction note explaining their significance and offering an AT that unpacks the honour being conferred (e.g. 'shall be granted high rank'). Separately, drinking from temple or sacred vessels in a profane banquet context is a symbolic act of mockery toward the God of that temple; add a note explaining the mocking significance. Overall survival rate: ~78% kept (22% deleted) per LAM+HAB data.
Context: ANE court regalia and profane sacred-vessel use as symbolic actions

Note: Name notes must identify WHO or WHAT the referent is — not just its grammatical category. Write 'the Babylonian name of Daniel' not 'the name of a man'; identify a place by its location or role ('a place near Jerusalem') not just 'a place'. For titles that function as names (e.g. Qoheleth), include the etymology and functional role: 'a title that means one who assembles a group.' Generic labels ('name of a man', 'name of a place') are consistently reworded by editors. Four editors across ZEC, DAN, and ECC applied this pattern.
Context: Specificity requirement for translate-names note content

Note: Deduplication rule: if figs-metaphor, figs-doublet, or another figure note already covers the same word or phrase in the same verse, drop the figs-idiom note for that phrase to avoid redundancy. Examples: a 'loosening of knots' idiom note was dropped once a figs-metaphor note addressed the same image; a 'make themselves hear' idiom note was dropped once figs-doublet and figs-explicit together covered the same phrase. Do not write competing notes for the same figure.
Context: Overlap deduplication: drop figs-idiom when figs-metaphor or figs-doublet already covers the same phrase

Note: DAN (Aramaic): the phrase כָּל קֳבֵל דִּי ('all before that') is an idiom whose meaning varies with context — it can mean 'because', 'therefore/so then', 'just as/in the same way as', or 'even though/although.' Every occurrence requires its own idiom note with a context-specific AT. Do NOT use a single generic AT across all occurrences; identify which meaning the idiom carries in each clause before writing the note.
Context: Aramaic idiom כָּל קֳבֵל דִּי — meaning varies by clause

Note: DAN (Aramaic): the term כְּעַן ('now' / 'and now') functions as a discourse-foreground marker signalling that the speaker is pivoting to their main point or a key directive — it is not purely temporal. Add a writing-foreground note explaining this function. Recommended ATs: 'So' for a single pivot; 'And so' when the speaker escalates to a climactic directive. This is distinct from the Hebrew הִנֵּה (behold) rule; both may coexist in the same chapter.
Context: Aramaic discourse marker כְּעַן — pivot-to-main-point function
